scaffold.description: How the write target was prepared. Required because `the manuscript is the tree this run may edit` is the one fact nothing downstream can re-derive — and the one a run gets wrong by pointing itself at a finished paper.

template_source.description: Where the class/style/bib files came from: a template package, a directory, or 'existing' when a scaffold was reused.

template.description: The class and version actually extracted, e.g. 'acmart v2.12 (2024/12/28), sigconf'.

created.description: The paths that make up the write target: what this stage created or extracted, or — when it adopted a tree the author had already built — the paths it verified are present. Empty only when the manuscript is an existing draft whose tree you did not enumerate.

reused_existing.description: True when the tree already existed and was adopted rather than scaffolded by this stage.

build_verified.description: Whether the compile command was run and produced a PDF. A claim you did not run is worse than a reported failure.

reference_disjoint.description: True only when no reference paper sits inside manuscript.root and manuscript.root sits inside no reference paper. When this is false the run spends hours improving a finished paper and every downstream check still passes.

layout_followed.description: Which reference repository's construction method was copied — one file per section? figures split into src/data/out? a plan/ dir? — and from where.

prompt_doc.description: The preparation document this run started from. Required so that 'no document existed' is a statement the result makes rather than a field it can omit, and so a reader can tell which values you were told from which you inferred.

path.description: Where you looked, whether or not it existed.

used.description: The brief fields whose values came from the document, e.g. core_claim, venue.page_limit, manuscript.state_dir.

conflicts.description: Where the document disagreed with the repository. Say which you kept and why; a document may deliberately describe a target state that does not exist on disk yet.

unresolved.description: Questions the document itself lists as open. They are already known to be undecided, so they are not worth asking again.

core_claim.description: The paper's thesis in one sentence. Every later stage must be able to check a paragraph against it.

template.description: The class/package the manuscript builds with, e.g. acmart-primary, ieeetran.

root.description: Directory containing the manuscript, resolvable from the working directory.

entry.description: The .tex file that is compiled, relative to root.

compile.description: The exact command that builds the PDF from root. Every writer stage runs it; it must already work.

state_dir.description: Directory, under root, where durable cross-round state lives (the reference spec, the storyline state). Required, because two agents guessing different defaults for it is how a loop loses its memory between rounds.

available_results.description: Result files that already exist and may be cited.

experiment_commands.description: Commands that regenerate the numbers. paper-audit uses these to validate a claimed value.

evaluation.description: Artifact that validates it, e.g. Fig. 5 / Tab. 2 / §5.1

reference_papers.description: Read-only standards for form. paper-calibrate measures these to derive the section budget, storyline arc, figure grammar and prose patterns this submission matches. Their content — numbers, claims, figures, prose — belongs to them and never enters this paper, and none of them may sit inside manuscript.root.

why.description: What this paper is the standard *for*: figure grammar, storyline arc, evaluation-table layout, prose. About form only.

read_only.description: Confirms it is a standard, not a workspace. Always true; present so a run that has confused the two cannot pass silently.

placeholders.description: Values the author has deliberately left unmeasured. Each one is a macro site in the manuscript — \ph{<id>} — and never a numeral, so that 'not yet measured' stays machine-distinguishable from 'invented'. paper-write emits the macro and reports it in placeholders_used; paper-audit counts the sites and refuses an unregistered one; paper-finalize will not report ready while any entry is open. The point is that the paper's gaps are a list a reader can see, rather than a number nobody can check.

id.description: The macro argument: \ph{ph-<...>}. Lowercase and hyphenated so site and registry line up textually.

what.description: The quantity that will go here, e.g. 'speedup when starting from a production FlashAttention-2 kernel'.

where.description: Where it appears in the paper: §5.4, Tab. 2 row 3, Fig. 6.

source.description: How it will be filled: the command to run, the workload to add, or the file it will arrive in. 'The author will fill it in' is not a source, because then nothing can ever check it.

status.description: open = the manuscript shows the macro at this site and no number.

filled_value.description: Only when status is 'filled': the value now in the manuscript and the file it came from.

constraints.description: Breaks found in the C→M→E mapping, budget pressure, or venue rules, stated plainly.

questions_asked.description: The questions actually sent to the author. Empty means every value came from the repository.

open_assumptions.description: Everything decided without being told. This is the loop's substitute for asking you again.

example.title_working: PIANO: a production-ready high performance kernel tuning agent with a programmable agentic workflow
example.core_claim: A workflow rather than a prompt is what makes an agent's kernel tuning reproducible: composing stages, loops and tournaments over interchangeable agent harnesses turns an open-ended optimisation attempt into a schedule whose every decision is recorded, contract-validated and re-runnable.

scaffold.layout_followed: Copied the construction method of the author's own paper repositories: an acmart main.tex with the class, bibliography style and refs.bib beside it, section bodies under sections/, a figures/ tree split into src/data/out so a plotted figure has a script and a data file behind it, planning notes under plan/, and a Makefile whose default target builds the PDF in one command. Structure only — no prose, number or figure was copied.

contributions.statement: A declarative workflow language in which agent stages compose through three node kinds — stage, loop and tournament — plus a feedback edge, and whose failure semantics (who owns the retry, what a round may leave behind) are part of the language rather than of the prompt.
contributions.evaluation: §5.2, §5.3: the same stage graph run as a serial pipeline and as a tournament, 7 paired configurations

contributions.statement: A harness abstraction that puts four different coding agents behind one event and resource surface, so a workflow names the harness per stage and the workflow itself stays model-agnostic.
contributions.evaluation: §5.4: the identical workflow executed under pi, claude and dsh

contributions.statement: An evidence chain that makes an agent's optimisation auditable after the fact: immutable handoff records, one result file per attempt, the full agent transcript, and a contract check with a bounded repair turn in place of silent acceptance.
contributions.evaluation: §5.6: the ledger of a single run read back and reconstructed

contributions.statement: An end-to-end result: agents given only a naive kernel and a benchmark entrypoint reach hardware-level throughput on a CUDA matmul, and the tournament node is what makes the outcome stable across models.

reference_papers.why: The closest systems paper of the author's own: the introduction's argument arc, the section budget of an acmart systems submission, and the figure grammar that pairs every plot with the script and data behind it.
The author's acmart sigconf typesetting standard: preamble and rights block, table style, and how a speedup claim is worded and scoped.
The evaluation-table layout and the win/loss framing used when a comparison does not go one way.

placeholders.what: speedup when the run starts from a production kernel instead of a naive one
placeholders.source: a from-production eval workload, to be added under evals/workloads/ and reported the same way as the from-scratch arm

placeholders.what: whether the same workflow reaches a comparable improvement on a second operator family
placeholders.source: a second tuning workload; until it exists the paper states one operator family and says so

placeholders.what: tokens and wall-clock per accepted round, against the improvement that round bought
placeholders.source: the per-run usage and timing already recorded in each eval report

constraints: One operator family (dense matmul) on one GPU: every claim in §5 is scoped to that, and the scope is stated in the abstract rather than left for the reader to discover.
The serial-versus-tournament comparison is a win on six of seven paired configurations and a loss on one; both are reported.
Do not turn a measurement the run did not make into prose. A sentence that would need ph-prod-speedup stays a \ph{} site with a note on what is missing.

unresolved: Whether a from-production arm will be run before submission, which is why ph-prod-speedup exists rather than a number.

open_assumptions: The section list was left to paper-calibrate, so the contribution-to-section mapping above is the document's target and may move by one subsection.
